summary: Defines SNMP managed objects for bridges, devices that connect separate LAN segments, based on what was then the draft IEEE 802.1d standard. It was later replaced by RFC 1493 and RFC 1525.

eli5.summary: A list of questions you can ask a network bridge, like how many messages it has passed along. It lets one program check bridges from many companies in the same way.

questions: how to manage lan bridges with snmp
how to manage network bridges with snmp
subtitle: SNMP objects to monitor and manage network bridges.

tldr.problem: Network administrators needed a standard way to monitor and manage network bridges—devices that connect separate LAN segments—across different vendors' equipment.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 1286 defines a set of SNMP managed objects (a MIB) organized into groups that cover bridge configuration, spanning tree protocol state, forwarding database operations, and traffic statistics.
tldr.outcome: This MIB became the foundation for bridge management but was replaced by RFC 1493 and RFC 1525 as bridge technology evolved.

today: RFC 1286 is obsoleted by RFC 1493 and RFC 1525, which provide more complete bridge management definitions. It is no longer the reference for bridge MIB management.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
A bridge is a network device that connects separate LAN segments below the network layer. It forwards frames from one segment to another based on their MAC addresses. RFC 1286 defines managed objects for administering bridges through SNMP, the Simple Network Management Protocol, permitting network operators to monitor and configure bridges from different vendors using a single standardized interface.

The RFC supports two major bridging modes: transparent bridging (where frames are forwarded based on learned MAC addresses) and source route bridging (where the sender specifies the path through intermediate bridges). Support for both approaches was essential for interoperability across the diverse networking landscape of the early 1990s.
sections.eli5: A bridge lets data hop between separate networks. This RFC explains how to check on a bridge's health and settings using standard SNMP questions, so a manager can monitor many bridges at once.

sections.title: MIB Structure and Groups
sections.content:
The Bridge MIB is organized into five main groups. The dot1dBase group is mandatory for all bridges and contains basic information: the bridge's unique address, the number of ports, and a table of statistics per port (frame discards due to delay or size). The dot1dStp group contains objects related to the Spanning Tree Protocol (if implemented), tracking the root of the tree, port states, and timers for topology changes.

The dot1dSr group manages source route bridging specifics such as hop count limits and routing information checks. The dot1dTp group covers transparent bridging: learning and aging of MAC addresses in the forwarding database, plus per-port frame and discard counters. The dot1dStatic group allows administrators to manually define which frames should be allowed to travel between specific ports.
sections.eli5: The MIB is like a filing cabinet with five drawers: one for basic bridge info, one for spanning tree (prevents loops), one for source routing, one for learning MAC addresses, and one for manual rules.

sections.title: Key Managed Objects
sections.content:
The base group includes simple counters and read-only objects. dot1dBaseBridgeAddress is the MAC address used to identify the bridge in spanning tree communications. dot1dBaseNumPorts reports the number of ports the bridge controls. dot1dBaseType indicates the bridging capability: transparent-only, source-route-only, or SRT (supporting both).

The Spanning Tree group includes read-write objects for administrators to tune timing parameters: dot1dStpBridgeMaxAge (how long to remember topology info), dot1dStpBridgeHelloTime (interval between status announcements), and dot1dStpBridgeForwardDelay (time a port spends transitioning between states to prevent temporary loops). These parameters apply when the bridge is the root of the spanning tree.
sections.eli5: Key measurements include the bridge's name (MAC address), how many doors it has, and timing knobs for the loop-prevention algorithm (if enabled).

sections.title: Forwarding and Learning
sections.content:
The transparent bridging group tracks the Forwarding Database (FDB), which records which MAC addresses have been learned on which ports. The FDB table stores the address, the port number where the address was learned, and the entry status (learned, static, or invalid). The dot1dTpAgingTime object sets how long a dynamically learned entry remains valid before expiring, allowing the bridge to detect when devices have moved or been unplugged.

The port table for transparent bridging provides counters for frames received and transmitted per port, as well as discards caused by the forwarding filter. The static table allows an administrator to specify addresses that should always be filtered to specific ports, overriding learned entries. This is useful for network policy enforcement and security.
sections.eli5: The bridge remembers which devices sit behind which doors by watching where frames come from. Administrators can also write down rules: 'never let this address through that door.'

sections.title: Management and Deprecation
sections.content:
RFC 1286 deliberately omitted some objects from the IEEE 802.1d standard because they were already covered by other MIB modules (such as MIB-II). For instance, the bridge name and uptime are retrieved from the system group, and port physical addresses come from the interfaces group. This design prevented duplication and encouraged consistent network management.

The RFC became quickly outdated as bridging evolved. RFC 1493 and RFC 1525 superseded it with more complete definitions of bridge management, incorporating lessons from implementation experience. Network operators should refer to those newer RFCs for bridge management today. The security section of RFC 1286 explicitly notes that security considerations are not discussed, reflecting the early SNMP era's lack of authentication.
sections.eli5: This RFC tried to avoid repeating facts that other parts of SNMP already knew. But as bridge technology grew, two better RFCs took its place—RFC 1493 and 1525.
